content:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: HelixBank x Redwood — Security review (RBAC, audit logs, separation of duties)
Date: 2025-02-06
Time: 18:30 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes

Attendees
- Redwood Inference: Markus Klein, Marcus Lin, Kevin Osei, Naomi Feldman
- HelixBank: Priya Desai (Security Architecture), Tom Alvarez (IAM Lead), Mei Chen (GRC / Compliance), Alex Rivera (Platform Engineering)

Auto-Summary (generated)
- HelixBank requested details on Redwood’s RBAC model (granularity, default roles, separation of duties) and audit logging for authorization decisions.
- Redwood described RBAC v2 primitives (resource/action/scope), default roles (Org Admin, Billing Admin, Security Admin, Developer, Read-only, Support/Impersonation), and approach to break-glass (time-bounded, audited).
- HelixBank emphasized SOC 2 / ISO evidence needs and SIEM export requirements, plus desire for custom roles.

Topics
- RBAC v2 structure: resources/actions/scopes
- Separation of duties: billing vs security vs platform ops
- SSO/SAML mapping (Okta groups → roles)
- Audit logs: authz decision context, retention, export
- Support impersonation and break-glass controls
- Private deployment considerations (policy distribution, air-gapped updates)

Questions (captured)
- Can we create a role that can export audit logs but cannot change billing?
- Do audit logs include “deny” events and the reason for denial?
- How do you handle emergency access (“break-glass”) and how is it monitored?
- Can roles be assigned at org and project scope independently?
- How is policy versioning handled across Private deployments (offline environments)?

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Cool, okay, I think we’re recording. Thanks everyone for jumping on. This is the security review follow-up. We’ll focus on RBAC and audit logs, separation of duties, and then any open items from the questionnaire.

[00:18] Priya Desai: Sounds good. Yeah, we’ve got compliance on as well because we’re mapping to our controls. We need to understand granularity and also what’s actually in the logs.

[00:30] Marcus Lin: Great. I’m Marcus, I lead product security here. Kevin’s on for audit logging specifics. Naomi’s PM for RBAC changes.

[00:41] Kevin Osei: Hey everyone.

[00:45] Mei Chen: Hi, thanks. For context we’re evaluating both hosted and potentially dedicated. Private is a later phase, but we need to know what differs.

[01:00] Markus Klein: Perfect. Maybe quick framing: today we’ll explain where we are with RBAC v2, what roles exist, what we can and can’t do with custom roles today, and then audit logs with auth decisions.

[01:13] Tom Alvarez: And SSO mapping. We’re Okta. Our concern is you say “roles” but we need group-based assignment and ideally project scoping.

[01:22] Markus Klein: Yep.

[01:24] Alex Rivera: Also operationally, who can rotate API keys, who can touch model deployments, and how do we keep billing separated.

[01:36] Naomi Feldman: That’s exactly the separation-of-duties stuff we’ve been standardizing.

[01:41] Markus Klein: Alright. Marcus, do you want to define the RBAC v2 model at a high level?

[01:47] Marcus Lin: Sure. So RBAC v2 for us is based on three primitives: resource, action, and scope. Resource is the object category (org, project, api_key, model_deployment, audit_log_export, sso_config, billing_profile, dedicated_capacity, things like that). Action is a verb (read, list, create, update, delete, rotate, export, impersonate, break_glass_grant). Scope is where it applies: org-wide or a specific project, and for some things we’ll scope down further like “deployment within project.”

[02:22] Priya Desai: When you say “will,” is that in production now or coming?

[02:27] Marcus Lin: In production we have RBAC today but it’s historically been coarse in places. The v2 work is to make checks consistent and auditable across control plane and console. Some endpoints already enforce v2 checks, some are in dual-evaluation mode right now.

[02:46] Mei Chen: Dual evaluation meaning you’re running both systems?

[02:49] Marcus Lin: Exactly. We evaluate v1 and v2 in parallel for a period. We can do “shadow deny” metrics—i.e. v2 would deny but we don’t enforce yet—so we can see if we’re going to break customers.

[03:07] Kevin Osei: And importantly, we log the decision metadata in a consistent way so you can later prove enforcement and debug.

[03:15] Tom Alvarez: Ok. But on the assignment side: can we say “Okta group A is Billing Admin,” “Okta group B is Security Admin,” etc.?

[03:25] Markus Klein: Yes for the default roles. You can map IdP groups/claims to roles. Today it’s typically SAML or OIDC claims mapping to role IDs at the org scope. Project-scoped role mapping is supported, but the UX is still evolving.

[03:43] Tom Alvarez: Do you support multiple roles per user?

[03:46] Marcus Lin: Yes. Users can have multiple role bindings. Effective permissions are the union, with explicit denies handled per policy semantics.

[03:56] Priya Desai: That’s a key detail. Is it deny-overrides or allow-only?

[04:00] Marcus Lin: In our current chosen semantics it’s primarily allow-based with explicit deny support reserved for a small number of cases (like preventing support impersonation in certain orgs), but generally we avoid complex deny logic because it’s hard to reason about. Most customers prefer allow-only plus strict defaults.

[04:22] Mei Chen: So if we don’t want support to impersonate, that’s a deny?

[04:26] Marcus Lin: That’s configured as an org-level setting and enforced as a hard restriction; we can represent it as a policy constraint too. For Private deployments, support impersonation is typically disabled by default.

[04:39] Alex Rivera: Can you talk about the default roles? Like what are the out-of-the-box roles and what can they do.

[04:45] Naomi Feldman: Sure. The default set we’re standardizing on is: Org Admin, Billing Admin, Security Admin, Developer, Read-only, and Support/Impersonation. Org Admin is full admin for the org. Billing Admin can manage billing details, invoices, usage limits, payment methods—without being able to change security settings like SSO or audit log destinations. Security Admin can manage SSO/SAML config, MFA requirements, audit log export configuration, and review audit logs. Developer can manage API keys and most project-level resources like model endpoints, rollouts, and environment settings—without billing or org security changes. Read-only is view access across most surfaces. Support/Impersonation is special and heavily gated.

[05:33] Priya Desai: When you say “audit log export configuration,” that’s sensitive. We require separation: someone can view logs but not change where logs are sent.

[05:43] Kevin Osei: Good callout. We split “audit_log.read” vs “audit_log.export.configure” vs “audit_log.export.run” as distinct actions in v2. Some customers want the “run export” permission for an analyst but keep “configure export destination” with a smaller admin group.

[06:02] Mei Chen: That’s exactly what we need for SOC evidence. Can you do that today?

[06:07] Naomi Feldman: For the defaults, Security Admin typically has those. If you want a narrower role (like “Audit Analyst”), that’s in the custom roles bucket. We can do limited accommodations in Dedicated/Private, but generally custom roles are on the roadmap with guardrails.

[06:27] Tom Alvarez: So no custom roles at GA right now?

[06:30] Markus Klein: Correct, not self-serve custom roles today. We’re trying to avoid a situation where everyone creates a bunch of roles without clear review/audit. We can work with you on a short list of additional default roles or a temporary policy bundle for Private, but we should treat it as an enterprise change.

[06:51] Priya Desai: Understood. We can live with defaults if separation is strong. Specifically: Billing admin cannot alter SSO; Security admin cannot change payment methods; Developers cannot change audit export destinations.

[07:05] Naomi Feldman: That’s aligned with how we’ve structured it.

[07:09] Alex Rivera: What about key management? Who can create API keys, rotate them, revoke them.

[07:15] Marcus Lin: Those are all separate actions under “api_key.*” and scoped at project. By default, Developer can create/rotate/revoke keys within their projects, Org Admin can do everything, Read-only cannot. You can also create a “Key Manager” persona if needed later, but again that’s custom role territory.

[07:38] Priya Desai: And can a Billing Admin see API keys?

[07:41] Marcus Lin: No, Billing Admin should not have visibility into secrets. They can see usage and invoices, but not secret material.

[07:50] Mei Chen: Good. Can you speak to audit logs: do you log all role changes and permission checks?

[07:57] Kevin Osei: We log role assignment changes (who granted what role to whom, at what scope). We also log access to certain sensitive surfaces. And we’re adding explicit authorization decision context for sensitive control plane actions: allow/deny, policy version, effective roles, and a reason code. For example, if someone hits “PUT /orgs/{id}/sso” we’d log something like decision=deny reason=missing_permission sso_config.update. If allowed, we log allow with the same context.

[08:29] Tom Alvarez: Do you log the denied actions too? Many vendors only log allowed.

[08:33] Kevin Osei: We log both for the sensitive endpoints. There’s some volume considerations, but for enterprise tenants we enable deny logging for admin/control plane actions. We don’t log every single read/list denial by default because it’s noisy.

[08:50] Priya Desai: That’s fine. We mostly need admin changes and access control changes.

[08:55] Mei Chen: Also retention. Our policy says 1 year online and 7 years archived, but we can accept export to our SIEM for long-term.

[09:05] Kevin Osei: Default retention in Redwood is shorter, but with SIEM export you can retain indefinitely on your side. We support export streaming, and in Dedicated/Private there are options to configure retention longer. For Private we can integrate with your logging stack (Splunk/Elastic) depending.

[09:25] Markus Klein: For Helix, I think you said you standardize on Splunk?

[09:28] Priya Desai: Splunk and sometimes Azure Sentinel, depends on the BU.

[09:32] Kevin Osei: We have an exporter that emits in a stable schema and we have mappings for common SIEM fields. I can send sample events so you can validate.

[09:44] Alex Rivera: What’s in the event? Like actor info? IP? session?

[09:49] Kevin Osei: Actor user ID, org ID, project ID if applicable, request ID, timestamp, source IP (where available), user agent, action/resource/scope, decision allow/deny, reason code, and policy version hash. For some actions, we include “target” identifiers like role_id assigned or api_key_id revoked (but never secret values).

[10:17] Priya Desai: Do you include the roles used in evaluation? We need to show “this decision was made because the user had Security Admin.”

[10:25] Kevin Osei: Yes, effective role IDs and role names, plus the policy bundle version. There’s also a correlation id so you can tie it to the underlying API call in app logs if you’re doing forensics.

[10:39] Tom Alvarez: Ok, and can we get the “why” beyond a code? Like human readable.

[10:44] Kevin Osei: We include a reason code (missing_permission, scope_mismatch, disabled_feature, break_glass_required, etc.). The UI can render it as readable. For raw events we keep it stable and machine-friendly.

[11:02] Markus Klein: Priya, can you share the key controls you’re mapping to? That might help us ensure we provide evidence.

[11:08] Mei Chen: For SOC2, it’s around logical access, least privilege, and monitoring. For ISO 27001 similar, but we also have internal policies about separation-of-duties.

[11:20] Priya Desai: And specifically, we’ve been burned by “Org Admin” being the only thing. We need at least Billing Admin separate, and we need audit log export separate from billing.

[11:32] Naomi Feldman: Totally. That’s why we created separate Security Admin and Billing Admin and are carving permissions to avoid “everything admin.”

[11:42] Alex Rivera: What about Dedicated capacity settings? Autoscaling, GPU pool, that kind of thing. Is that separate?

[11:49] Marcus Lin: In Dedicated we treat those as “dedicated_capacity.*” actions. Typically restricted to Org Admin and a limited Ops Admin persona. We’re careful because it impacts cost and availability. We can keep those out of Developer by default.

[12:07] Priya Desai: That’s good. We want platform engineering to manage scaling, but not billing, and not SSO.

[12:15] Markus Klein: So you might end up with Billing Admin, Security Admin, and Platform Admin (or Org Admin restricted to a small group). Today “Platform Admin” is basically Org Admin, but we can discuss if the default “Developer” + dedicated capacity admin actions cover it.

[12:34] Tom Alvarez: If we can’t create custom roles, we need the default roles to meet our SoD. Can you send the role matrix?

[12:40] Markus Klein: Yes, we’ll send the RBAC v2 overview and the role definitions matrix. It lists each role and which actions it covers.

[12:49] Priya Desai: Thank you.

[12:52] Markus Klein: Switching to break-glass: Priya, you asked in the questionnaire about emergency access and support.

[12:59] Priya Desai: Yes. We need to know: does Redwood staff have standing access to customer orgs? Is impersonation possible? How do you do approvals.

[13:09] Marcus Lin: No standing access by default. Support access is controlled and time-bounded. For sensitive actions, we use an elevated session model (break-glass). It requires an approval flow (depending on severity), is limited duration, and generates explicit audit events: grant, use, and revoke/expire. We also alert internally on usage.

[13:36] Mei Chen: Is that customer-visible?

[13:38] Marcus Lin: Yes, for enterprise you’ll see audit log entries showing support access being granted and what actions were taken.

[13:46] Tom Alvarez: For Private deployments, can you disable support impersonation entirely?

[13:51] Marcus Lin: Yes, and it’s generally the recommended default. For Hosted/Dedicated, you can restrict it; for Private it can be disabled at install time or policy level.

[14:04] Alex Rivera: When you say “install time,” does that mean it’s a config in the private control plane.

[14:08] Marcus Lin: Correct. Private has a policy bundle distribution model, so the same RBAC primitives apply, but the customer controls the environment. We sign policy bundles and can provide updates, but you can pin versions.

[14:23] Priya Desai: Pinned versions matter for audit. We need to know policy changes are controlled.

[14:28] Kevin Osei: That’s why policy version is in the audit event. You can prove which policy was active at the time of a decision.

[14:39] Mei Chen: How do you prevent someone from changing the policy to grant themselves access and then changing it back.

[14:46] Marcus Lin: Policy updates are privileged and audited. In Hosted, customers can’t modify the underlying policy bundle, only assign roles within it. In Private, policy bundle updates are an administrative operation and should be guarded by the highest privilege and operational controls.

[15:05] Tom Alvarez: Do you have a concept of “two-person rule” for policy changes?

[15:09] Marcus Lin: We don’t have a built-in 4-eyes approval for policy changes today. For Hosted it’s moot since customers don’t change policy. For Private, we recommend customers use their change control process and restrict who can apply upgrades. We can provide guidance.

[15:27] Priya Desai: That’s acceptable for now for Private, as long as it’s documented.

[15:32] Markus Klein: On custom roles: Naomi, can you say where we’re heading and what we can commit.

[15:38] Naomi Feldman: Directionally we’re building custom roles, but phased. First we’re shipping consistent permissions and defaults, plus a permission inventory governance. Then we add the ability to compose roles from actions, with guardrails (like warning on high-risk permissions). The timeline is still being finalized; we can follow up offline with what we can support during your evaluation.

[16:07] Mei Chen: Understood. For our procurement, we need something in writing: “supports separation of duties with Billing Admin and Security Admin.”

[16:14] Markus Klein: We can provide that statement along with docs. We’ll send the RBAC v2 overview.

[16:22] Priya Desai: Another question: Can you scope roles to projects? We have multiple teams. We can’t have one developer see everything.

[16:31] Marcus Lin: Yes. Role bindings can be applied at project scope. Common pattern: org-level Security Admin is small group; project-level Developer is team-specific.

[16:45] Alex Rivera: And who can create projects.

[16:47] Marcus Lin: That’s an org-level permission. Usually Org Admin or a limited admin role.

[16:54] Tom Alvarez: Okta mapping: if we add a user to an Okta group, how quickly does it apply?

[17:00] Markus Klein: Near real-time on next login / token refresh. For active sessions, depends on session length. We can also force re-auth for sensitive changes.

[17:12] Priya Desai: You should log role changes and group mapping changes, correct?

[17:17] Kevin Osei: Yes. Role assignment changes are logged. SSO config changes are logged. Group mapping changes (like claim mapping) are also logged because it affects access.

[17:31] Mei Chen: Good. Now, audit logs. Do you have an API for pulling them or only exports.

[17:38] Kevin Osei: Both. There’s an API to query recent events (with pagination) and there are export mechanisms for long-term. For SIEM we recommend export.

[17:51] Tom Alvarez: Are the audit logs immutable?

[17:54] Kevin Osei: In Hosted, yes from a customer perspective—you can’t edit them. Internally we treat them as append-only with access controls. In Private, immutability depends on your storage backend, but we can recommend WORM-compatible storage.

[18:14] Alex Rivera: Does Redwood log the actual request payloads? Like prompts, etc.

[18:20] Markus Klein: For inference payloads, we have data retention controls and by default we don’t store prompts long-term unless configured for debugging. For audit logs we’re talking about admin/control plane events, not prompt content.

[18:34] Priya Desai: Just to confirm, this RBAC applies to the control plane mostly. What about data plane calls, inference endpoints.

[18:42] Marcus Lin: Great question. Data plane is scoped by tenant/project API keys. That’s the primary auth boundary. RBAC v2 is mostly for control plane actions like managing keys, models, deployments, org settings.

[18:58] Priya Desai: Okay.

[19:00] Mei Chen: On SOC evidence, we’ll need sample screenshots or sample log events. Can you provide a sample.

[19:08] Kevin Osei: Yes, I can provide sample JSON events (redacted) showing allow and deny with the authz decision fields.

[19:16] Markus Klein: And we can also provide docs and, if needed, a short walkthrough in Console once you’re in the pilot.

[19:26] Tom Alvarez: Another separation-of-duties issue: can Billing Admin change usage limits which might affect availability.

[19:33] Naomi Feldman: Billing Admin can change billing profile and payment method, and may be able to set spend limits or budgets depending on plan. But autoscaling and capacity changes are separate and not under Billing Admin.

[19:51] Alex Rivera: But budgets could effectively DOS a project by setting it too low.

[19:56] Naomi Feldman: True. We treat that as a billing/financial control. Some customers want a “Finance” team to control that. If you need a separate “Budget Admin” we can discuss, but again it’s beyond current defaults.

[20:13] Priya Desai: In our model, finance can do that. It’s okay, but we need it clearly documented.

[20:20] Markus Klein: We’ll flag that in follow-up.

[20:23] Mei Chen: Switching to policy governance: how do you ensure new endpoints don’t bypass RBAC.

[20:31] Marcus Lin: We’re adding conformance tests in CI that require endpoints to declare a permission and have the authz check wired. That’s part of the governance. Also periodic inventory review.

[20:46] Priya Desai: Good. We’ve had vendors that ship features without updating roles.

[20:51] Marcus Lin: Same concern. That’s why we’re formalizing it.

[21:00] Tom Alvarez: Okay, can you explain error handling. If someone lacks permission, what do they see.

[21:06] Markus Klein: They get a 403 with a reason code and message in the UI. We avoid leaking sensitive details.

[21:14] Alex Rivera: Is the reason code stable? We integrate with tooling.

[21:18] Kevin Osei: Yes. Reason codes are versioned and we aim to keep them stable.

[21:26] Priya Desai: Nice.

[21:28] Markus Klein: Let’s talk Private briefly since it came up. You said it’s phase two but you need to know whether RBAC exists there.

[21:38] Priya Desai: Right. If we do Private, it might be in an environment with restricted outbound internet.

[21:45] Marcus Lin: Private supports offline/air-gapped options. The RBAC policy bundle is packaged as a signed artifact. Updates are applied through your upgrade process, not fetched ad-hoc.

[22:02] Tom Alvarez: And if policy bundle is outdated, do we get version skew issues.

[22:06] Marcus Lin: We design the services to be compatible with a bounded range, but yes version skew is something we actively manage. That’s part of why policy version is explicit.

[22:19] Mei Chen: That’s enough for now, thank you.

[22:23] Markus Klein: Coming back to your immediate blocker: can we satisfy your enterprise questionnaire item: “Fine-grained RBAC with separation of duties and audit logs.”

[22:33] Priya Desai: We need: (1) documented role definitions, (2) documented audit log contents including authz, (3) confirmation of break-glass controls.

[22:44] Markus Klein: Great. We can provide all three.

[22:48] Kevin Osei: I’ll send the audit log schema examples. I’ll include a sample for role assignment change and a sample for denied SSO config change.

[22:59] Naomi Feldman: I’ll provide the role matrix; Marcus can send the overview.

[23:05] Marcus Lin: Yep.

[23:07] Alex Rivera: Quick one: can read-only see billing usage.

[23:10] Naomi Feldman: Read-only can see usage dashboards depending on configuration, but not invoices or payment details. Billing Admin is required for that.

[23:22] Priya Desai: That’s fine.

[23:24] Tom Alvarez: And do you have API access to role assignments so we can reconcile with our IdM.

[23:31] Markus Klein: Yes, there are admin APIs to list role bindings. In Private you can also integrate directly. We’ll include endpoints in the follow-up.

[23:45] Mei Chen: Ok.

[23:47] Markus Klein: I’m going to jump to recap and next steps, unless there are more security items.

[23:55] Priya Desai: One more: do you support SCIM.

[23:58] Markus Klein: For provisioning we support SCIM for enterprise plans. It helps keep users and groups in sync.

[24:06] Tom Alvarez: Great, that’s required.

[24:10] Markus Klein: Awesome.

[24:12] Markus Klein: Recap: Redwood will send the RBAC v2 overview, plus the default role definitions matrix. Kevin will send sample audit log events including authorization decision context and policy version. We’ll also answer the questionnaire items in writing, including break-glass / support impersonation defaults, and confirm what’s configurable in Private.

[24:35] Priya Desai: And we’ll send you our role separation list and our Okta group structure.

[24:42] Tom Alvarez: Yeah, I’ll send the claim mapping details.

[24:46] Mei Chen: And we’ll schedule a 30-minute follow-up for Private policy distribution.

[24:51] Markus Klein: Perfect. Thanks all.

[24:55] (Call continues with light scheduling / calendar logistics; transcript truncation due to diarization)

[25:03] Speaker 1: Next week Tuesday maybe.

[25:07] Markus Klein: Yeah I’ll send options.

[25:11] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[25:13] Call ended (per Fireflies)

Note: Fireflies transcript shows early end due to speaker diarization; meeting duration per calendar was 56 minutes. Remaining time was primarily scheduling and a short walkthrough of where audit logs appear in the console (no new security commitments).
